newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Worrying trends emerge in Bosnia economy-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Worrying trends emerge in Bosnia economy-analysts.

text.p: Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation economy showed worrisome trends in May with inflation on the rise and industrial production declining in the last two months, a World Bank analyst said on Tuesday.

The state Statistics Bureau has reported a 2.9 percent rise in retail prices in May and April as well as a decrease in industrial production of 1.3 percent in May and a 7.5 percent fall in April, raising concern among foreign economic experts.
"You can have monthly fluctuations in inflation, but still, two months of close to three percent of inflation is worrying," the analyst, who asked not to be named, told Reuters.

Four currencies are employed in Bosnia: Yugoslav dinars in Serb territory, Croatian Kuna in Croat areas, Bosnian dinars in Moslem-controlled areas and the German mark serving as the de facto common denominator.

The data formally pertains to the federation's currencies -- the kuna and Bosnian dinar -- but actually reflects Bosnian dinar inflation. Printing and issuing of the Bosnian dinar is directly linked to foreign currency reserves.

The expert, who analyses the federation data every month, said the cause of the inflation trend was unclear and said it could be merely the lack of a seasonal adjustment applied to economic statistics.
A joint currency fully backed by foreign reserves is supposed to be introduced later this year, pending negotiations on currency design between rival political leaders.
Federation industrial output showed a substantial slowdown, partly due to a fall in electric power production and coal mining, he said.

The federation economy grew at a 50 percent rate last year, fuelled by more than a billion dollars in reconstruction aid. The World Bank has estimated the economy will probably grow at a steady 35 percent in the next few years.
A deceleration in growth was expected but not a decline in production, the analyst said.

Much of the federation's growth has come from donor funds for emergency repairs of damaged infrastructure. Having in mind the low starting point for the war-damaged economy, the growth figure falls far behind developed countries' growth rates.
Bosnian Serbs saw only two percent of an estimated $1.2 billion committed in Bosnia in 1996 and marginal growth as a result of their failure to comply with the peace agreement.
Bosnia's peacetime government, comprised of former enemies, bowed to international pressure last week and endorsed a package of economic laws prescribed by the international financial authorities.
The legislation cleared the way for negotiations with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) on a stand-by agreement and $100 million in assistance over a one year period.
The IMF deal should clear the wary for a donors' conference for mid-July sponsored by the World Bank and the European Union, which is expected to raise $1.4 billion for reconstruction in 1997.

Bosnia's Serb entity, which covers half the country, will be receiving substantial reconstruction aid this year for the first time and its economy is expected to catch up somewhat with the federation as a result, the analyst said.
"External assistance from the World Bank and other donors is already picking up quite sharply and the (upcoming) donors' conference will give it another kick," he said.
"But even then the growth rate won't come even close to the federation's, because the Serb economy has been in dire straits for so long."
